source_text: Τί μοι λοπὸν καταλέγειν τὸ πλῆθος ὦν σέβονται ζώων Αἰγύπτιοι, ἑρπετῶν τε καὶ κτηνῶν καὶ θηρίων καὶ πετεινῶν καὶ ἐνύδρων νηκτῶν, ἔτι δὲ καὶ ποδόνιπτρα καὶ ἤχους αἰσχύνης; Εἰ δὲ καὶ Ἕλληνας εἴποις καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἔθνη, σέβονται λίθους καὶ ξύλα καὶ τὴν λοιπὴν ὕλην, ὡς ἔφθημεν εἰρηκέναι, ἀπεικονίσματα νεκρῶν ἀνθρώπων. Φειδίας μὲν γὰρ εὑρίσκεται ἐν Πείσῃ ποιῶν Ἠλείοις τὸν Ὀλύμπιον Δία, καὶ Ἀθηναίοις ἐν ἀκροπόλει τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν. Πεύσομαι δέ σου κἀγώ, ὦ ἄνθρωπε, πόσοι Ζῆνες εὑρίσκονται· Ζεὺς μὲν γὰρ ἐν πρώτοις προσαγορεύεται Ὀλύμπιος καὶ Ζεὺς Λατεάριος καὶ Ζεὺς Κάσιος καὶ Ζεὺς Κεραύνιος καὶ Ζεὺς Προπάτωρ καὶ Ζεὺς Παννύχιος καὶ Ζεὺς Πολιοῦχος καὶ Ζεὺς Καπετώλιος. Καὶ ὁ μὲν Ζεὺς παῖς Κρόνου, βασιλεὺς Κρητῶν γενόμενος, ἔχει τάφον ἐν Κρήτῃ· οἱ δὲ λοιποὶ ἴσως οὐδὲ ταφῆς κατηξιώθησαν. Εἰ δὲ καὶ εἴποις τὴν μητέρα τῶν λεγομένων θεῶν, μή μοι γένοιτο διὰ στόματος τὰς πράξεις αὐτῆς ἐξειπεῖν (ἀθέμιτον γὰρ ἡμῖν τὰ τοιαῦτα καὶ ὀνομάζειν), ἢ τῶν θεραπόντων αὐτῆς τὰς πράξεις ὑφ᾿ ὧν θεραπεύεται, ὁπόσα τε τέλη καὶ εἰσφορὰς παρέχει τῷ βασιλεῖ αὐτή τε καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ αὐτῆς. Οὐ γάρ εἰσιν θεοί, ἀλλὰ εἴδωλα, καθὼς προειρήκαμεν. ἔργα χειρῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ δαιμόνια ἀκάθαρτα. Γένοιντο δὲ τοιοῦτοι οἱ ποιοῦντες αὐτὰ καὶ οἱ ἐλπίζοντες ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς.
pass_a_gloss: What to me to speak the multitude of which Egyptians reverence living things and reptiles and beasts and wild animals and birds and aquatic swimming things, and still also foot-basins and shameful sounds? If indeed you would say also Greeks and the other nations, they reverence stones and wood and the rest of matter, as we have said before, images of dead men. For Phidias is found in Pisa making for the people of Elis the Olympian Zeus, and for the Athenians on the acropolis the Athena. I will ask you, man, how many Zeuses are found: for Zeus is called first Olympian and Zeus of Lateum and Zeus of Casius and Zeus of Ceraunius and Zeus the Forefather and Zeus All-Night and Zeus Guardian of the City and Zeus of the Capitol. And the Zeus who is the child of Cronus, having become king of the Cretans, has a tomb in Crete; but the rest perhaps were not deemed worthy even of a burial. But if you would say the mother of the so-called gods, may it not be for me to speak through my mouth her actions (for it is unlawful for us to even name such things), or the actions of her attendants by whom she is attended, as many as fees and contributions she and her sons provide to the king. For they are not gods, but idols, as we have said before. They are works of human hands and unclean demons. May those who make them and those who hope in them become such.

pass_b_english: Why should I go on listing the countless living things the Egyptians worship—reptiles, livestock, wild beasts, birds, and every kind of aquatic creature—along with foot-basins and shameful noises? If you point to the Greeks and the other nations, they worship stones, wood, and the rest of matter: images of dead men, as we have already said. Phidias, for example, is found in Pisa crafting the Olympian Zeus for the people of Elis, and the Athena on the Acropolis for the Athenians. Let me ask you, then: how many Zeuses can be found? Zeus is called first Olympian, then Zeus Latearius, Zeus Cassius, Zeus Ceraunius, Zeus Propator, Zeus Pannychius, Zeus Poliouchus, and Zeus Capitolinus. The Zeus who is the son of Cronus became king of the Cretans and has a tomb in Crete; the rest perhaps were not even deemed worthy of burial. If you were to name the mother of the so-called gods, may I never be forced to speak her deeds with my mouth—for it is unlawful for us even to name such things—or the deeds of her attendants by whom she is served, or the many fees and contributions she and her sons pay to the king. For they are not gods, but idols, as we have said before; they are works of human hands and unclean demons. May those who make them and those who hope in them become like them.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek text. Pass A provides a literal gloss, and Pass B provides a fluent English rendering that preserves all nuances, including the list of Zeus epithets, the distinction between the various types of animals, and the parenthetical remark regarding the unlawfulness of naming the mother of the gods. The translation of 'Γένοιντο δὲ τοιοῦτοι οἱ ποιοῦντες αὐτὰ καὶ οἱ ἐλπίζοντες ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς' as 'May those who make them and those who hope in them become like them' correctly interprets the optative expressing a wish/curse.
